title: Cyprus Parliament Reviews Reports on Abramovich-Linked Asset Transfers
content:
The Cypriot Parliament this week discussed recent revelations about corporate maneuvers that allowed firms ultimately owned by Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich to sidestep tax and transparency requirements.

The parliamentary hearings followed an investigation last week by OCCRP, CIReN, BBC, and TBIJ. The reports detailed how the Cyprus affiliate of multinational accountancy firm Deloitte, and corporate service provider MeritServus, worked together to backdate documents relating to companies beneficially owned by Abramovich. 

Doing so helped the companies retroactively transfer billions of dollars in assets from Cyprus to the British Virgin Islands, where they would not be subject to Cypriot laws on tax and public disclosure. 

OCCRP reached out to Deloitte’s offices in Cyprus and internationally for comment on the parliamentary hearing, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. Deloitte Cyprus previously told OCCRP it "acts in compliance with applicable laws."

MeritServus has been dissolved and it was not possible to obtain a comment.

title: Many in Serbia’s Youth Movement Fear a Rigged Election on Sunday
content:
Riding an extraordinary wave of public mobilization, Serbia’s student-led opposition heads into Sunday’s snap parliamentary election genuinely believing it can break President Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year grip on power.

Yet beneath the euphoria of this week’s mass rallies lies a pervasive conviction among its supporters that the contest will be anything but fair—and that the ruling party will resort to outright ballot theft rather than concede defeat.

On Thursday night, that tension was on full display as hundreds of thousands of people flooded into Belgrade’s central Slavija Square, filling the surrounding boulevards in a buoyant, flag-waving display of collective defiance. The assembly marked the movement's final campaign rally ahead of an early vote that serves as the culmination of nearly two years of youth-led unrest against Vučić’s rule.

What began in November 2024 as grief and outrage following the collapse of a newly renovated railway station canopy in the northern city of Novi Sad—a disaster that killed 16 people and was turned by the protesting youth into a lethal symbol of state corruption and crony contracting—has since metastasized into a nationwide rebellion.

title: Sanctioned Investor in Cambodian Scam Compound Owns California Mansion
content:
Brendon Luo was sanctioned in June by the U.S. Treasury Department, which alleged he was an investor in a cyber-scam compound operated by Cambodia's Prince Group. Property records show he still owns a mansion in a gated community in southern California.

The Prince Group is widely accused of involvement in compounds in Cambodia where thousands of trafficked workers were forced to commit industrial-scale cyberfraud. The Prince Group has strongly denied the accusations, but the U.S. has sanctioned more than 140 allegedly-associated entities and individuals, including Luo.

The sanctions have not disrupted Luo’s ownership of a five bedroom mansion in Yorba Linda, a city of about 68,000 people that is part of the Los Angeles metropolitan area. Although no sale price was identified in property records, online real estate portals value the property at roughly $5 million.

Luo was born in China and acquired passports from Cambodia, Vanuatu and Cyprus, according to information from sanctions notices as well as immigration records obtained by OCCRP.

title: US Court Orders Lebanese Ex-Minister to Pay $35M in Torture and Fraud Case
content:
A U.S. district court has ruled against four Lebanese individuals, including a former minister, finding them liable for fraud, torture and civil conspiracy and ordering them to pay $35 million in damages, for orchestrating the kidnapping and torture of a Lebanese-American couple.

Speaking to OCCRP about the verdict from the Florida court, Lara Samaha, a U.S. green card holder, said the couple filed in the U.S. because “the justice system in Lebanon is so corrupt it is impossible to obtain justice.”

According to the default final judgment seen by OCCRP, a binding court order issued when defendants fail to respond to a lawsuit, the court ordered Gebran Bassil—a sitting member of parliament, Lebanon’s former foreign minister, and the son-in-law of former President Michel Aoun—to pay millions in damages, along with three co-defendants.

“⁠I feel justice has been served after 7 years in court and more than 300 court filings,” Lara Samaha told OCCRP. She confirmed that there will be a follow up on a related lawsuit in Lebanon, though she declined to detail the next steps.

title: Cambodia Cracked Down on Banks Allegedly Linked to Cyber-Scams. The IMF Says the Problem Persists.
content:
Amid mounting international pressure to clean up its financial system, Cambodia’s central bank published a statement earlier this month accusing unnamed actors of waging a campaign of “economic sabotage” against the country.

“Rumors and unverified information have been circulating on social media, claiming that a number of banking and financial institutions are facing issues or heading toward collapse in the near future,” the National Bank of Cambodia (NBC) said.

The NBC did not clarify who might be behind such a campaign, or which institutions were targeted. But the regulator warned that such “baseless” information could undermine “trust in the overall banking system.”

The banking system has taken a beating recently, as international attention turned to Cambodia’s role as a major hub for cyber-scams targeting victims around the world. Proceeds from scams have allegedly flooded into financial institutions.

title: EU Sanctions Envoy Pushes for Action Against Rusal’s Irish Alumina Refinery
content:
Material produced in a major metals refinery in Ireland is “undoubtedly” going into Russia’s weapons supply chain, the European Union’s Sanctions Envoy David O’Sullivan said on Thursday, adding that “there is a very real issue to be addressed.”

The comments, made at the Institute for International and European Affairs (IIEA) in Dublin, come seven months after OCCRP and partners published an investigation showing that the Aughinish Alumina refinery in western Ireland was indirectly supplying Russian weapons producers.

As much as half of the alumina from the Aughinish refinery was shipped to smelters owned by its parent company, United Company Rusal, and used to produce aluminum. The metal was then sold to a trading company supplying dozens of EU-sanctioned Russian weapons manufacturers, OCCRP’s investigation showed. 

Weapons made by these firms have leveled entire city blocks in Mariupol, struck a children’s hospital in Kyiv, and blown open an apartment building in western Ukraine, according to EU sanctions listings, Ukraine’s military intelligence, and the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

title: Smugglers Collected Up to $509M on Europe Routes in 2025
content:
Smugglers netted an estimated $388 million to $509 million from sea crossings to Europe in 2025, according to new research by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). The agency estimated that between 190,000 and 209,000 people were smuggled along four major Mediterranean and Atlantic routes, with criminal networks facilitating between 57 percent and 90 percent of departures. Fees varied widely depending on the journey, ranging from $170 for crossing to Spain’s Canary Islands to more than $7,500 for routes toward Italy and Malta, according to the International Organization for Migration.

The Central Mediterranean was the busiest route, with up to 100,400 people smuggled, followed by the Eastern Mediterranean with up to 51,300, the Northwest African Atlantic route with 33,000, and the Western Mediterranean with 24,500. These estimates, according to UNODC, reflect all smuggling attempts, including journeys that ended in interception or tragedy. The routes remained deadly: 3,404 people died or went missing in 2025, while another 104,200 were intercepted at sea and returned.

title: Interpol Cybercrime Crackdown Nets 1,400 Arrests and $105M
content:
Interpol announced Thursday that authorities from 21 countries across Africa have arrested 1,462 suspects linked to cross-border cybercrime networks in what it described as “one of Africa’s largest cybercrime enforcement operations.” The agency said the operation disrupted 10,909 malicious networks and led to the recovery of more than $105 million in illicit funds.

Law enforcement identified 65,929 victims targeted by these  cybercriminal networks, with investigations linking the criminal activity to losses exceeding $385 million. In Uganda alone, authorities dismantled two transnational fraud rings, arresting 365 foreign nationals linked to online investment and pension fraud schemes targeting victims across Asia.

title: From Flights to ‘Incentives,’ Indonesian Nickel Giant Harita Approved Payments for Local Politicians and Leaders
content:
When senior mining executive Stevi Thomas was convicted alongside an Indonesian governor for bribery in 2024, the ruling was seen as a rare case of accountability for corruption in the Southeast Asian nation. 

The court case revealed how the politician had received some $60,000 in bribes for facilitating permits for Harita Group, a conglomerate that has sourced up to eight percent of the world’s nickel supply in recent years  — and has also left a trail of environmental damage in its wake. 

Now, leaked internal records obtained by OCCRP reveal a host of other payments that Harita executives earmarked for local politicians, individuals identified by the firm as community leaders, and the military between 2013 and 2023. 

The planned or approved payments amounted to at least $389,000 and took the form of flights for politicians, “incentives” for the community leaders, and financial support for military projects. 

Evidence of these outlays was found in leaked company emails, internal memos, and invoices.

Reporters were unable to independently verify if the money was ultimately disbursed in every instance, or establish the precise purpose of some of the approved payments.

title: Collapsed Surrogacy Agency Loses U.S. Civil Case After Court No-Show
content:
Collapsed international surrogacy agency World Center of Baby has been dealt a double blow in Florida, with a judge ruling against its U.S. corporate entity in a civil lawsuit – shortly after another case against the company was filed.

The developments come just over a month after OCCRP published a global investigation into the chaos World Center of Baby left in its wake after announcing it was filing for bankruptcy, including surrogates left unpaid and unsupported, and prospective parents abandoned. 

In a decision made publicly available on Tuesday, Judge Thomas Ramsberger in Florida’s Sixth Circuit Court ruled in favor of a U.K.-based couple who brought a case against the agency’s U.S. corporate entity World Center Group Corp and two of its representatives. The complaint was on five counts, including breach of contract and fraud. 

The lawsuit accused the company of “a calculated and coordinated scheme” to secure substantial payments for promised services despite its worsening financial and operational problems.

title: In a Vienna Bakery, Fresh Pastries and a Backdoor for Serbian Votes
content:
For the ordinary Viennese, it’s just another neighborhood Balkan bakery.

But to the more than 76,000 Serbians living in the Austrian capital, the shop known as Pekarica — "little bakery" — offers a fragrant touch of home, where orders are exchanged effortlessly in their native tongue as the scent of dough wafts from the oven.

That’s not all. On one recent morning, a customer stepped to the front of the counter, ignoring the steaming trays of braided breads and glossy pretzels entirely.

“Excuse me,” he said. “I was told by my colleagues that I can register to vote here.”

“Yes, you can,” the clerk replied, unfazed by the question. “Not here exactly, but further down. Come, I’ll take you.”

She led him out the door and a few steps down the pavement to the modest storefront housing the Association of Serbs in Austria. Inside, the walls were plastered with campaign posters, slogans, and portraits of Serbia’s long-serving president, Aleksandar Vučić, and his ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
snippet: For the ordinary Viennese, it’s just another neighborhood Balkan bakery.

title: Liechtenstein Discontinued Investigation into Swiss Banker
content:
In 2023, OCCRP reported that Venezuela’s former head of the treasury under President Hugo Chávez had been under investigation in Liechtenstein for allegedly laundering money using gold bars.

Reporters found that investigators had also looked into Swiss banker Ronnie Budja, but could not confirm whether he faced any charges.

Liechtenstein authorities have since confirmed that an official investigation into Budja was discontinued in 2024 due to insufficient grounds to initiate criminal proceedings.

title: Albanian PM Offers Dialogue Amid Crackdown on Violent Protests
content:
After months of public unrest and more than a week of escalating anti-government protests, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has called demonstrators to the negotiating table, setting up chairs labeled "DIALOGUE" at the bottom of the stairs leading into the government building. 

"Now, whoever wants unconditional dialogue, wherever they want, whenever they want, even here if they want, I am available along with the Government," Rama said in a video posted to Facebook on Tuesday. "The only ones who are not welcome are those who commit violence and those who do not distance themselves from violence."

The overture comes as student-led demonstrations enter their eighth day, with crowds demanding Rama's resignation over allegations of widespread corruption. During a meeting with education officials, Rama characterized the recent unrest as a "hybrid war," claiming that foreign and political actors are exploiting genuine economic concerns to incite violence and attempt to overthrow the government.

Meanwhile, the streets of Tirana have seen severe clashes, with demonstrators throwing stones and firecrackers at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons.

title: South Pacific Ponzi Scam “King” Noah Musingku Dies
content:
A fugitive South Pacific Ponzi scammer—who later proclaimed himself “king” of a remote armed territory at the center of Papua New Guinea’s Bougainville island—has been given a royal burial following his death from an unspecified illness, according to local media and photographs of the funeral posted on social media.

Noah Musingku was accused of stealing tens of millions of dollars from victims across the region in a 1990s pyramid scheme known as U-Vistract. Following the collapse of the scheme, Musingku fled in the early 2000s to his home island of Bougainville, a region then still recovering from a devastating decade-long civil war.

Styling himself as King David Peii II of the twin kingdoms of Papaala and Me’ekamui, Musingku set up a pseudo-state with its own armed militia, banking system, and local currency known as the Bougainville kina (BVK). The BVK was later declared illegal by Papua New Guinea’s government.

title: Kazakh President’s Grandnephew Donates Sport University to State Following Investigative Report
content:
Just one day after an investigation by Radio Azattyq and OCCRP, the grandnephew of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced on Saturday that he is donating the Kazakh National University of Sports (KNUS) to the state.

Framing the handover as a patriotic gesture, Nurassyl Medeu stated the move was not a sale, a transfer into trust management, or a forced step, “but a gratuitous gift to my native country so that it prospers, reaches unprecedented heights, and achieves recognition at the global level.”

“Everything we created must serve our youth, our people, and our country,” he said, adding that it was a great honor to make the contribution. “If you compare KNUS to a ship, I built it to be powerful, reliable, and unbreakable.”

The unexpected announcement of Medeu followed a Friday investigation revealing Medeu to be the grandson of President Tokayev’s sister, Karlyga Izbastina, and detailing how two major educational ventures he founded received substantial state support.

title: Five Questions About What’s Behind Nigeria’s Romance Scam Industry
content:
In February, OCCRP tracked down a 31-year-old man to his mansion in Nigeria’s capital Abuja. He had allegedly posed as the Crown Prince of Dubai to con a Romanian businesswoman out of more than $2.5 million in a romance scam, according to his victim and two accomplices. 

This is a well-trodden profession in Nigeria, where large numbers of young men, often facing extreme poverty, have taken to swindling lonely victims in wealthier countries to fill their pockets.  

Yet most of the romance scams originating in Nigeria are not particularly complex or lucrative, says journalist Carlos Barragán.

His recently published book, “The Yahoo Boys,” explores what drives the country's teenage fraudsters — whose nickname comes from the Yahoo email addresses used for “Nigerian prince” scams in the early days of the internet — and the repercussions of their scams in Nigeria and abroad.

title: Romanian Institutions Bought Banned Russian Cybersecurity Software
content:
More than 80 Romanian public institutions continued to purchase cybersecurity software from a Russian-founded company after the government explicitly banned its use over national security concerns, a review of public procurement records reveals.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania passed a 2022 law prohibiting public entities from acquiring cybersecurity software originating fromRussian individuals or entities. In March 2023, a government order officially blacklisted a broad range of products from Kaspersky, a Russian cybersecurity firm.

However, procurement data shows that between March 2023 and September 2026, 83 public institutions and authorities made 131 purchases of prohibited software.

In an emailed statement, Kaspersky said it “does not have any inappropriate ties to any government.” 

“Kaspersky has maintained that the claims about alleged security risks that the company’s products might have and related restrictions are based on the current geopolitical climate rather than a technical analysis of Kaspersky software security,” the company said.

title: Scammers in Timor-Leste Go Straight Back to Work After Being Busted, Police Say
content:
Foreign scammers arrested in Timor-Leste are returning to their illicit activities after being convicted in local courts and paying modest fines, police say, highlighting the challenges the tiny Southeast Asian country faces combatting a surge in cyberfraud operations. 

As an example of the problem, a spokesperson for the National Police of Timor-Leste cited the 18 foreign nationals detained last month in raids on two alleged scam centers in the country’s capital, Dili, that police announced on social media.

According to the police announcements, all arrested in those raids had previously engaged in similar criminal activities and “been processed under the law in force. Timor-Leste police spokesman Angelo Quelo told OCCRP that some of them had even been arrested and convicted twice before.

“If people commit a crime twice or third [time], then we should send them to prison,” Quelo said in an interview with OCCRP this week. 

Among the 18 suspects, 14 had been released after each paying a fine of $3,000, while the other four suspects were released after their charges were dismissed, he said.

title: A 23-Year-Old Kazakh Owns Two New State-Backed Universities. He’s the President’s Great-Nephew.
content:
Declaring 2026 the “year of artificial intelligence,” Kazakhstan’s president is in the midst of an ambitious drive to transform the Central Asian nation into a “digital state,” with AI at the center of the effort.

Two weeks after creating a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence in September 2025, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced the next prong of his government’s agenda: setting up an AI research university, which would be granted “special status.” 

That initiative is now in full swing. And the company tapped to spearhead the project was founded by Tokayev’s 23-year-old great-nephew, before a state institution acquired shares in the venture, an investigation by Radio Azattyq has found.

Qazaq AI Research University, which opened its doors to students last month, is one of two universities that were founded by Nurassyl Medeu, the grandson of Tokayev’s sister, and now have significant state support, company filings and open-source records show.

title: Jaguar Trafficking in Latin America Persists Through Bone Paste and Pet Smuggling
content:
Skins in markets, fangs turned into jewelry, and bones processed into paste: the illegal trade in jaguars persists in Latin America. An investigation spanning seven countries points to a primarily local, small-scale business, with evidence of international trafficking in Peru and Suriname.

Between 2023 and 2025, the Wildlife Justice Commission (WJC) investigated the trade of these big cats in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Panama, Peru, and Suriname. Its findings—shared with OCCRP—describe a market that often relies on sporadic sales opportunities, though the investigation also identified a network trafficking multiple species.

The latest WJC report "The Illegal Jaguar Trade in Latin America: An Updated Picture," published Thursday, found that a significant portion of the demand stems from local buyers, including members of Asian communities residing in the region. These results add nuance to alarms raised in the early 2010s regarding a new international market for jaguar parts targeting China, while not ruling out the continued existence of those connections.

title: Interpol Operation Nets 95 Arrests for Child Abuse
content:
An international operation coordinated by Interpol has resulted in the arrest of 95 individuals suspected of producing and distributing child sexual exploitation and abuse material. According to a Thursday statement, the six-month operation, conducted between March and September 2026, spanned 17 countries across Latin America and Europe.

Authorities targeted platforms and cryptocurrencies used to groom children, coordinate abuse, connect offenders, and receive payments for illegal content. Of the arrested suspects, 89 percent were male and 11 percent were female. Among those detained are the parents of a five-year-old victim, accused of producing and selling abuse material of the child online.

title: Chaos in Tirana: Violent Student Protests Surge
content:
Prime Minister Edi Rama addressed youth protesting in Tirana on Thursday for the first time after three days of violent demonstrations, calling them the country’s future and urging dialogue, while insisting that genuine students were not responsible for the widespread destruction.

Speaking in a video message recorded inside the damaged offices of the European Union-backed College of Europe in Tirana, Rama drew a sharp line between student concerns and the street violence that has paralyzed parts of the capital.

"Students are the future... and for them, we are always ready to sit down, speak, discuss, and find solutions," Rama said. However, he accused political opponents of hijacking the demonstrations, calling the attacks on public institutions the work of "an opposition which, hiding behind blind masks, seeks with fire and iron to drag Albania back into the abyss". Warning that the law applies to everyone, Rama vowed that anyone responsible for the devastation "will pay".

title: UK Freezes £30 Million Mansion Linked to Alleged Senior Prince Group Associate
content:
The United Kingdom this month issued an asset freeze order on a £30 million ($39 million) mansion near Holland Park, central London, belonging to alleged senior Prince Group associate Hu Xiaowei, records reveal.

According to filings submitted to the U.K.’s Land Registry on October 5, the property was officially frozen in connection with the country’s March 2026 designation of Hu Xiaowei as a sanctioned individual and asset freeze target.

Hu Xiaowei did not respond to OCCRP’s request to comment for this article. 

OCCRP has reported extensively on Hu Xiaowei, including unmasking his multiple identities and his portfolio of global assets, including the Holland Park mansion.

Following allegations he held a senior role in Prince Group,  he has also been sanctioned by the United States, and been subject to asset freezes in Hong Kong, as well as a money laundering investigation in Singapore. Additionally, he has been indicted in Taiwan.

Now largely shuttered as a result of sweeping sanctions, Prince Group was a multi-billion dollar Cambodian conglomerate that allegedly secretly operated as one of Asia’s largest organized crime groups.

title: Five Arrested in 1 Million Euro Fraud Against NATO
content:
European authorities arrested five people in Norway and raided properties in Germany and Romania as part of an investigation into a company suspected of defrauding NATO member countries of more than 1 million euros ($1.11 million), Eurojust said Wednesday. The targeted company and its subcontractors allegedly provided shore-based support—known as husbandry services—to NATO military vessels visiting ports in northwestern Europe.

The network is accused of submitting fraudulent invoices and using an intermediary to bribe foreign public officials to secure favorable contracts with the alliance. NATO's procurement agency, the NSPA, discovered the billing anomalies, triggering a cross-border probe in April 2025. Eurojust noted that the exact financial loss is still being calculated by the joint investigation team, which involves anti-corruption police and prosecutors from Norway, Romania, Germany, and the U.K.

title: Russia Detains Japanese Journalist on Espionage Charges
content:
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, accusing him of collecting defense-related information for a Japanese intelligence agency. The reporter was detained Tuesday in the far eastern Sakhalin region, a day before he was due to leave the country, according to a Tuesday statement by the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB). The journalist was transferred to Moscow where a district court ordered his pretrial detention.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the journalist as Yuki Imai, a correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper. Confirming the espionage charges, she claimed Tokyo is using credentialed reporters to gather intelligence and said the incident would further damage bilateral relations, which have deteriorated over the war in Ukraine and Japan’s military policies.

title: Bank of America Fined $1.21B Over AML Failures
content:
U.S. authorities imposed more than $1.21 billion in penalties on Bank of America on Tuesday over failures in its anti-money laundering controls and apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, in what the Treasury Department called the third-largest enforcement penalty in its history.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty, saying the bank failed to adequately detect and report financial activity involving priority national-security and illicit-finance risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity along the U.S. southwestern border. Regulators said Bank of America failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including more than $1 billion linked to such priority risks.

As part of the FinCEN resolution, Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act, including by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required due diligence on correspondent accounts for foreign banks, and file suspicious activity reports. The bank must also use an independent third party to identify and report suspicious activity its systems previously missed.

title: Convicted Belgian Cocaine Boss Poured Millions Into Luxury Dubai Properties
content:
Belgian drug lord Nasserdine Tarrahi, who has been convicted of drug-related offenses in three separate cases, was extradited from Dubai to Belgium on October 14, the Antwerp prosecutor’s office confirmed to OCCRP and De Tijd. 

Tarrahi, 38, was a senior figure in the “Turtles,” a Belgian-Moroccan gang that specialized in retrieving South American cocaine from containers passing through the port of Antwerp. Later in his career he fled to Dubai, where he continued to run drug trafficking operations from the Emirati city-state, according to the most recent court verdict against him, issued in May. 

But although Belgian justice has finally caught up with him, authorities have struggled to confiscate the proceeds of his crimes, which a court in Antwerp estimated could amount to 5 million euros ($5.5 million). They only managed to find the equivalent of around $20,000 in cash, plus an assortment of exercise equipment crammed into an apartment in Antwerp he used as a base for drug trafficking.

title: The Maldives Plans to Offer Residency to the World’s Ultra Rich – And Create Islands From Scratch to Do It
content:
Once an isolated haven for scuba divers searching for technicolor marine life, the shallow turquoise waters of the Noonu Atoll in the Maldives are in the midst of a makeover.

A fleet of dumper trucks, excavators, forklifts, and cranes has moved into the habitat for protected parrot fish and nurse sharks to sculpt 25 artificial islands and islets from over six million cubic metres of sand dredged from the seabed. 

Known as Project Ayla, the $790 million private development will host over 70 luxury dwellings and represents the vanguard of a new government strategy to lure the high-net-worth crowd to the debt-saddled nation. 

A view of the main worksite island for Project Ayla in July 2026. CREDIT: Hassan Moosa/Maldives Independent

Yet beyond the plumes of coral-smothering sediment churned up by the dredgers, opposition politicians and transparency advocates are warning of an even murkier threat: the prospect of a new international tax shelter and potential money-laundering hub carved from the ocean floor.
snippet: Once an isolated haven for scuba divers searching for technicolor marine life, the shallow turquoise waters of the Noonu Atoll in the Maldives are in the midst of a makeover.

title: Hackers Turn French Supermarket Refrigerators Into Furnaces
content:
A massive cyberattack targeted hundreds of French supermarkets overnight on October 11 to 12, remotely hijacking refrigeration systems to trigger intense defrost cycles, spoiling vast quantities of food and sparking fires.

The unprecedented incident has triggered a national criminal investigation. The Paris Prosecutor's Office confirmed to OCCRP Tuesday that its cybercrime section has initiated an investigation, entrusted to the Anti-Cybercrime Office (OFAC). The probe aims to "identify the victims and establish a link between the incident and the damage reported by them, specifically regarding food spoilage and the outbreak of fires."

Hackers gained remote control of the store refrigeration systems by exploiting internet-connected controllers. The attack methodology mirrors vulnerabilities the operational technology security firm Claroty warned the industry about two months prior. In a prescient August report titled "Freeze the Controller, Defrost the Food," the firm's Team82 research division warned about the possibility that hackers could access Danfoss refrigeration systems to bypass security and manipulate temperatures.

title: UK Sanctions Dutch Businessman Allegedly Linked to Russian Arms Firms
content:
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions⁠ on Dutch businessman Alexander Tattersall and his Turkish company, Redwing Metal, following a joint investigation by The Kyiv Independent, OCCRP and IrpiMedia that exposed shipments of European industrial equipment to Russian factories supplying missile and fighter jet manufacturers.

Tattersall and Redwing Metal were among 38 individuals, companies and vessels targeted⁠ by the British government on October 8 as part of a broader effort to disrupt Russia’s military supply chains, oil revenues and financial networks.

The measures freeze assets under British jurisdiction and prohibit British individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with the designated parties.

The sanctions follow a June investigation⁠ by OCCRP, The Kyiv Independent and Italy’s IrpiMedia, which revealed that Redwing Metal had shipped more than $5 million worth of European-made industrial machinery to two Russian metallurgical plants in 2023 and 2024, despite EU export restrictions.

The equipment included computer-controlled lathes, metal heat-treatment furnaces, hydraulic presses and other machinery manufactured in Italy, Germany, Spain and the Czech Republic.

title: EU Blacklists Nearly 1,600 in Russian Defense Firms and Executives
content:
The European Union adopted its largest-ever single set of sanctions against Russia to date on Monday, blacklisting 1,569 individuals and companies within the country's military-industrial complex.

The measures blacklist 826 Russian companies and 743 chief executives, bringing the total number of listings under the EU sanctions regime protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity to nearly 4,600. The designated entities face immediate asset freezes and funding blocks, while the targeted individuals are now barred from entering the bloc.

The package specifically targets mid-level suppliers that form the "core" of Russia's defense sector, which together generate an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros ($22.32 billion) and employ more than 250,000 people.

According to the European Council, the designated companies supply critical components for advanced weapons systems, including semiconductors, radars, satellite systems, explosives, and optics. Notably, more than half of the new listings address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses in its daily strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure.
snippet: The European Union adopted its largest-ever single set of sanctions against Russia to date on Monday, blacklisting 1,569 individuals and companies within the country's military-industrial complex.

title: Croatia Expands Probe Into Alleged Multi-Million-Euro Toxic Waste Scheme
content:
Croatia's anti-corruption office, USKOK, expanded its investigation into an alleged international illegal waste dumping ring, arresting and questioning five new suspects and three companies over the suspected criminal disposal of hazardous materials near the town of Benkovac and inside the Velebit Nature Park near Senj.

The suspects were released after questioning, as USKOK stated there were no legal grounds to request pre-trial detention. Friday's action marks the third expansion of the sweeping environmental crime probe, which now targets a total of 14 individuals and four companies suspected of severe environmental crimes and falsifying official documents within a criminal enterprise.

The investigation, supported by Europol and law enforcement from Italy and Slovenia, became public in February 2025 with the initial arrest of 13 people. Authorities dismantled an alleged criminal network that is accused of orchestrating the illegal import of hazardous waste from Germany, Italy, and Slovenia into Croatia.

title: A Chinese Auto Giant Sponsors Portugal's National Football Team. Its Trucks Are Used by Russia to Attack Ukraine.
content:
As part of its “Vast Ocean Plan” for global expansion, one of China’s largest automotive companies recently announced its sponsorship of Portugal’s national football team.  

“Europe stands as a strategic priority,” Changan Automobile said in a press release in May, adding that its partnership with the Portuguese Football Federation offered a new opportunity for “brand engagement across the region.”

In an earlier phase of a global push by the state-owned company, Changan moved into Russia. Later, as international car makers left following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Changan started exporting more vehicles to fill the gap in the market, according to the industry analysis group inovev. 

Reporters found that some of those vehicles have been used in Russia's war against Ukraine, as launchpads for models of drones known to have attacked both military targets and civilians.

Changan Automobile did not respond to requests for comment. 

The Portugal Football Federation said the contract with Changan was signed after being reviewed for “the tight Federation compliance rules.”
snippet: As part of its “Vast Ocean Plan” for global expansion, one of China’s largest automotive companies recently announced its sponsorship of Portugal’s national football team.

title: Fiji Criticized in U.S. Trafficking Report Over Failure to Tackle Grace Road Cult
content:
Fiji has been granted a one-year reprieve from a potential downgrade that could lead to U.S. aid cuts, amid concerns over its efforts to combat human trafficking, including its response to the Korean doomsday sect the Grace Road Group, according to a U.S. State Department report released last week.

This year’s Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report kept Fiji on its “Tier 2 Watchlist” of countries that do not fully meet the State Department’s minimum standards for combating human trafficking, noting that the Pacific island nation had failed to secure a trafficking conviction for three years running.

“Official complicity and corruption undermined anti-trafficking efforts and allowed traffickers to operate with impunity” in Fiji, the Oct. 8 report found.

However, the State Department granted Fiji a one-year waiver sparing it from being automatically downgraded to Tier 3, a designation that would have put it alongside countries including Iran and Afghanistan and could result in restrictions on U.S. non-humanitarian assistance.

Fiji, a country of just under a million people, has been on the Tier 2 Watchlist since 2024, but last year’s TIP report was the first to single out Grace Road.

title: Hungarian Ad Agency Got Millions From Firm Owned by Orban’s Billionaire Friend
content:
Just a few years after launching in 2020, Megafon Digital Incubator Center had become one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of the ruling party and its leader, Viktor Orbán. 

But Megafon appears to have lost its sense of purpose since Orbán was swept from power in national elections this past April. Four months after that stunning loss, its website was taken offline.

Now, internal documents from a firm called V-Híd Zrt reveal the source of much of Megafon’s income. Around $12 million in donations came from that company, which is owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, Orbán’s childhood friend. 

Mészáros became fabulously wealthy during Orbán’s 16 years in power, building a business empire spanning sectors from construction to banking and energy. Mészáros’ companies won seven percent of all public procurement contracts — together worth about $2 billion — between 2018 and 2020 alone, according to Transparency International.

title: Deloitte’s Cyprus Office Helped Abramovich Firms Relocate Billions in Assets in Apparent Bid to Sidestep Tax and Transparency
content:
The Cyprus affiliate of multinational accountancy firm Deloitte signed off on backdated paperwork for companies beneficially owned by Roman Abramovich, which helped the firms retroactively transfer billions of dollars in assets from Cyprus to the British Virgin Islands (BVI) to try to get around tightening tax and transparency laws, leaked files show.

By piecing together years of email correspondence and financial records, reporters found that in the mid-2000s Deloitte Cyprus discussed and helped to execute the transfer of assets — including bank deposits, yachts, and luxury real estate — in the wake of increased taxes and transparency requirements on foreign-owned and private firms in Cyprus ahead of its accession to the European Union in 2004.

Deloitte Cyprus worked closely on the plans with MeritServus, a now-U.K.-sanctioned Cypriot corporate services provider that was a division of Deloitte Cyprus before it was spun out as an independent firm in 2005.

The two firms advised senior staff at Millhouse Capital U.K. Limited, a firm managing assets owned by Abramovich, and Millhouse LLC in Russia.

title: Montenegro Arrests then Expels Russian 'Rybar' Network Leader, Associates
content:
Montenegrin authorities detained on Friday five persons believed to be the leaders of the Russian media and influence network "Rybar," which Western security agencies view as a sophisticated tool for Kremlin influence operations.

Prime Minister Milojko Spajić framed the action in a post on X as a national security and foreign interference operation.

Spajić noted his government had previously warned of "attempts at hybrid action and destabilization of Montenegro" as the nation pursues European Union integration. Cautioning against "hasty statements," the Prime Minister stated that "serious indications" require every lead to be thoroughly investigated within a broader security context.

"Institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will endanger our European future," Spajić wrote.

Montenegrin daily Vijesti cited the Montenegrin Police Directorate as stating the arrests were carried out with the support of "international partners" in order to neutralize illegal activities.

title: Kidnappings and Home Invasions Soar as French Syndicates Extort Crypto
content:
A father beaten and forced into a car trunk. A magistrate and her mother held hostage for 30 hours. A family terrorized overnight in northern France for digital cash. Over the past two years, a violent wave of kidnappings and home invasions has swept across France targeting cryptocurrency executives, influencers, and their loved ones, as criminal networks increasingly turn to physical torture to extort digital fortunes.

Organized criminal networks increasingly turn to home invasions, physical torture, and abductions to extort digital fortunes. Authorities have recorded 77 such incidents so far this year, up from 67 in 2025 and roughly 20 in 2024, according to data from France’s National Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime, known as PNACO.

While the early wave of violence primarily targeted high-profile industry executives and wealthy influencers, law enforcement officials warn that criminal syndicates are increasingly hunting ordinary citizens suspected of holding digital wallets. Just weeks ago, four armed intruders held a family captive overnight in the northern town of Vendin-le-Vieil, forcing the father to hand over about 40,000 euros, or $47,000, in cryptocurrency.

title: Lithuanian Minister Condemns Intimidation Campaign against Investigative Reporters
content:
Lithuanian Culture Minister Lukas Alsys condemned the harassment of journalists and editors on Thursday after being asked about growing pressure on 15min staff following the news outlet’s joint investigation with OCCRP into the crypto-finance firm Bankera.

“Any persecution of journalists or editors aimed at intimidating or frightening them is completely intolerable,” Alsys told Žinių Radijas, adding that relevant authorities should “draw conclusions.”

The joint investigation revealed that more than 45 million euros raised during Bankera’s 2017–2018 token sale was transferred to Pacific Private Bank in Vanuatu, an offshore entity acquired by Bankera’s three co-founders. Records showed the bank subsequently issued millions of euros in loans to the founders and their companies, including funds used to purchase luxury real estate.

Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service opened a pre-trial investigation shortly after the story was published in April 2025. Vanuatu’s central bank later revoked Pacific Private Bank’s international license, though the decision was stayed pending appeal.

What followed was a systematic campaign of pressure targeting journalists and executives at 15min.

title: IKEA Stopped Selling in Russia. But its Former Belarusian Supplier Filled the Gap — With Strikingly Similar Furniture
content:
When the Swedish furniture giant IKEA exited Russia and Belarus in 2022 in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it instructed its suppliers to do the same. A Lithuanian supplier complied, and stopped sourcing IKEA products from its Belarusian factory.

But the Belarusian factory didn’t stop exporting furniture after losing the rights to IKEA designs. Instead, it appears to have filled an IKEA-shaped void in the Russian market, exporting pieces that are strikingly similar to the Swedish designs.

The website of one Russian retailer even told customers that “IKEA's departure doesn't mean you have to give up your familiar interior design style,” adding that they “now have the opportunity to buy those same beloved products.”

“Yes, their appearance and names have changed slightly,” the blurb on the website said. “But the design, quality, ease of purchase, and ease of assembly remain unchanged.”

IKEA said it could not comment on individual cases, but noted that it “continuously monitors potential infringements” on its intellectual property rights.

title: Nearly 50 Arrested as Police Target Western Balkan Drug Network
content:
Nearly 50 suspects have been detained following an international crackdown on a Western Balkan drug syndicate allegedly linked to murders, kidnappings, and grenade attacks across Europe, Europol announced on Thursday.

The multi-year investigation culminated on October 6, when police searched 42 properties across Slovenia and Spain. Law enforcement arrested 36 suspects on the action day—34 in Slovenia, one in Spain, and one in Croatia—adding to 11 members previously detained during the probe.

The syndicate comprised nationals from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Türkiye, and the Netherlands. To move cocaine, cannabis, amphetamine, MDMA, and methamphetamine from Belgium, the Netherlands, and Spain to destinations across Europe, the group allegedly hired drivers—chiefly from Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Bulgaria—to conceal illicit cargo within regular commercial shipments using trucks, vans, and cars.

title: Georgia Scraps Offshore Intermediary in Azerbaijani Power Imports
content:
Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia will eliminate intermediary companies from its electricity imports from neighboring Azerbaijan, a move he said would save the state millions of dollars annually.

The trade has long been plagued by a lack of transparency, with power purchases between the two South Caucasus nations funneled almost entirely through opaque offshore companies, as previously reported by OCCRP and its regional partners. For years, the dominant player in the trade was Sulkhan Papashvili, an influential Georgian businessman.

“Having an intermediary meant additional costs for the state,” Kobakhidze said during a recorded cabinet meeting. “Specifically in the case of Azerbaijan, as a result of removing the intermediary, the state will receive several million annually.”

In 2020, Studio Monitori, OCCRP’s Georgian member center, reported that ordinary Georgians were paying inflated rates for Azerbaijani power due to the middleman arrangement — at the time handled by a Belize-registered firm, Elgreen Holdings.

title: Police Say Scam Center Busted in PNG Had Moved from Cambodia
content:
A suspected online scam operation that was raided by police in Papua New Guinea last month is believed to have relocated to the Pacific island country in response to a crackdown on online fraud in Cambodia, local police have told OCCRP.

So far four Chinese citizens have been charged with human trafficking offences over the alleged scam center, which operated out of a luxury residential complex in PNG’s capital, Port Moresby. Police rescued 39 Indonesian workers in the raid who are suspected of being held against their will.

The suspected Port Moresby scam operation is the first of its kind in Papua New Guinea, a resource-rich but underdeveloped country of 11 million people. Experts have warned that small and poor states across the globe are at risk of turning into new bases for Asian syndicates that profit from the world’s $1 trillion a year online scam industry.

Cambodia has for years served as a center for massive scam compounds, many of which rely on trafficked workers, but international pressure since late last year has led the country’s authoritarian government to turn against the illicit industry. Thousands of scam operators have since left the country.

title: U.S. Designates China-Born Businessman in Fiji for "Significant Corruption"
content:
The U.S. State Department announced Thursday it had designated for “significant corruption” Zhao Fugang, a Chinese Communist Party-backed businessman in Fiji that OCCRP has previously revealed to be a top organized crime target of Australian law enforcement.

Zhao, a China-born Fiji citizen, is a leading member of the Pacific island country’s Chinese business community and heads the Overseas Chinese Service Center in the capital, Suva. OCCRP and Australia’s Nine media have previously reported that Australia placed the businessman on its top tier list of criminal targets in 2023 on suspicion that he is a senior member in a syndicate involved in drug smuggling, money laundering, and human trafficking.

Zhao has not been charged with a crime and no evidence has been publicly presented against him. He denies any wrongdoing.

The State Department said in a statement that Zhao had “abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business and criminal interests.” The designation restricts Zhao or his family members from entering the U.S.

title: Azerbaijan Denies Link to Espionage Case Involving Former German Spy Chief
content:
Azerbaijan has denied a report from a German magazine that claimed a former German spy chief — arrested Tuesday on treason and espionage charges — used classified state secrets to prepare an “analysis” for Baku’s intelligence services in exchange for money.

The denial follows a Tuesday statement from Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office announcing the arrest of August Hanning, who served as President of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005. Police also arrested his former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D.

Prosecutors accuse Hanning of procuring “nearly two thousand documents, many of which contained classified information,” with the help of Manfred D., in “exchange for payment,” from 2010 to 2022. While Hanning had by then retired from public service, Manfred D. worked as chief of staff for several subsequent BND heads from March 2012 to March 2026.

Hanning allegedly “commercially exploit[ed]” this classified information in his private consulting work. In one instance, prosecutors allege he used state secrets to draft an “analysis” for an unnamed foreign intelligence agency.

title: The Uzbek President’s Son-In-Law Secretly Acquired a UAE Passport While Serving as a Top Security Chief
content:
At the 2023 UN climate change conference in Dubai Otabek Umarov watched in the wings as his boss, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, met with his United Arab Emirates (UAE) counterpart.

Sporting a crisp navy suit and tie, Umarov at the time was the second most important official charged with protecting the Uzbek president. Perhaps more importantly, he was –– and remains –– married to Mirziyoyev’s youngest daughter, and is widely seen as an influential behind-the-scenes power broker.

But on that December day in Dubai, Umarov carried a potentially career-ending secret: seven months earlier, he had covertly obtained an Emirati passport requiring his sworn fealty to the state led by the man his father-in-law was talking to, President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.

Uzbek military law governing the security post Umarov occupied at the time prohibited his second citizenship, and would have served as possible grounds for discharge from active duty.
snippet: At the 2023 UN climate change conference in Dubai Otabek Umarov watched in the wings as his boss, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, met with his United Arab Emirates (UAE) counterpart.

title: Ex-Ukrainian Lawmaker Sent to Trial Over $1.3 Million Fraud Scheme
content:
Ukrainian anti-corruption authorities have sent a case to trial charging former lawmaker Heorhii Lohvynskyi and five others with misappropriating 54.18 million hryvnias (about $1.3 million) in state funds and laundering the proceeds.

Investigators allege that between 2013 and 2016, Lohvynskyi organized a scheme involving Golden Mandarin Oil LLC and a debt dispute with energy company Kyivenergo. The group allegedly used a fraudulent "friendly settlement" at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) to trick the Ukrainian government into paying off a private corporate debt with public money.

According to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), a representative of Golden Mandarin Oil applied to the ECHR seeking payment from the state over a debt Kyivenergo allegedly owed under a 2009 domestic court ruling. Investigators say the company concealed from the ECHR that the legal right to claim the debt had already been transferred to a third party.

title: Montenegro Moves to Seize Vast Real Estate Empire of Fugitive Crime Boss
content:
Authorities in Montenegro might not be able to catch the country's most notorious fugitive crime boss, but they are moving to dismantle his financial empire.

The Special State Prosecutor's Office asked Tuesday the High Court in Podgorica to permanently confiscate a sprawling portfolio of real estate and luxury vehicles it believes is in his or his wife’s possession. While the official statement only identified the targets by their initials, R.Z. and his wife, T.Z., the request appears to be detailing the hidden wealth of the reputed Kavač clan leader Radoje Zvicer and his wife Tamara Zvicer. Local media reports also name the two as the targets of this request.

The timing of this massive forfeiture request is no coincidence. It serves as one of the first major tests of Montenegro's sweeping new "Anti-Mafia Law," passed on September 4. The government hailed the legislation as a "historic step" that has already caused an "earthquake in criminal circles," specifically because it empowers the state to permanently confiscate assets in organized crime cases even before a final judicial verdict is reached.
snippet: Authorities in Montenegro might not be able to catch the country's most notorious fugitive crime boss, but they are moving to dismantle his financial empire.

title: Cocaine Boatmen Are Being Blown Up By US Airstrikes, But The Drugs Keep Flowing From Colombia
content:
First, you hear the high-pitched whine of drones overhead. Next comes the boom of explosions.

“And then in the following days, the sea brings in a jerrycan, pieces of a boat, drugs, people too,” says Alberto, a local businessman living on the Colombian peninsula of La Guajira.

This grim sequence of events has become familiar for those based along this arid strip of desert, whose shores are lapped by a part of the Caribbean Sea that has been the site of some 20 deadly U.S. strikes on speedboats over the past year.

The U.S. military campaign against the alleged “narco-terrorists” manning these vessels, known as Operation Southern Spear, has faded from headline news since the first attack was launched over a year ago on September 2. 

Yet it continues to destroy small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific — with at least 235 dead in some 70 strikes so far — in the face of heavy criticism from legal experts and rights groups, who call it an ineffective program of what are essentially extrajudicial murders.

title: Prosecution of Tren de Aragua Accused Mastermind Deemed Complex Case
content:
A suspected cybercriminal who allegedly bankrolled the notorious Tren de Aragua gang through a multimillion-dollar ATM fraud scheme was arrested and will remain behind bars to face a complex prosecution in Nebraska, just days after the Venezuelan was blacklisted by the Treasury Department.

In a news conference Saturday in Omaha that began with, “well we got him,” FBI Special Agent in Charge Eugene Kowel said Anibal Alexander Canelón Aguirre, an alleged computer whiz and hacker tied to the transnational gang, was captured on the high seas.

During his news conference, Kowel said the FBI in Omaha received assistance from the U.S. Coast Guard and the FBI's Critical Incident Response Group. Canelón Aguirre, he said, was subsequently transported by sea and air to the District of Nebraska.

The FBI’s web page for its most-wanted fugitives now shows a red bar across his photo reading “Captured.”

title: Leaked Video of Uruguayan Kingpin Triggers Mass Arrests Across Bolivian Justice System
content:
Even from inside an American prison cell, the Uruguayan drug kingpin Sebastián Marset managed to shatter the highest echelons of Bolivian justice this week.

The sudden release on Wednesday of two video recordings from Marset’s arrest in March sparked a sweeping law enforcement purge, leading to the detention of 14 high-ranking figures — including prosecutors, police commanders, the country’s attorney general, and the former national director of Bolivia’s special counter-narcotics unit.

The operation included raids on prosecutorial offices in Sucre, La Paz, and Santa Cruz after the newly surfaced video footage showed Marset claiming that the attorney general, Roger Mariaca, and other top law enforcement figures had shielded his criminal syndicate.

Bolivia’s Minister of Government, Marco Antonio Oviedo, described the operation as the dismantling of a “criminal organization entrenched in the justice system” that was dedicated to “protecting, encouraging, and supporting narco-terrorism.”

title: EU Froze Sierra Leone Aid for Harboring Alleged Drug Kingpin, Netherlands Says
content:
The European Commission has suspended nearly $20 million in aid to Sierra Leone’s 2026 budget due to the West African country’s harboring one of Europe's most wanted fugitives, alleged cocaine kingpin Joseph "Jos" Leijdekkers, Dutch Justice Minister David van Weel said Thursday.

Posting on social media from the EU’s Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting, van Weel wrote: “At the JHA Council meeting in Luxembourg, discussions are focusing on European security, the EU sanctions regime for organized crime. A positive development in this context is that the EU will no longer provide budget support to the authorities of Sierra Leone this year.”

Later in the day, he told Dutch public broadcaster NOS that the EU had suspended 18 million euro (roughly $20 million) in aid to Sierra Leone because the West African country is not cooperating with the Netherlands’ extradition request of Leijdekkers, a Dutch citizen.

Courts in the Netherlands and Belgium have handed Leijdekkers more than 100 years in prison sentences in absentia in convictions for a range of crimes, including drug trafficking, assault, armed robbery, and attempted murder.

title: Amnesty Report Documents Morocco's Sustained Spyware Campaign Against Civil Society
content:
Amnesty International has released a new report showing how, despite official denials, Moroccan authorities used surveillance spyware against civil society between 2017 and 2021, and possibly continued to use it later. 

The rights watchdog’s report, titled “We start with the verdict”: Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine, details how the government deployed Israeli firm NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware to target civil society figures both domestically and abroad in what Amnesty described as “unlawful surveillance attacks.”

“The report presents extensive technical and forensic evidence confirming the DGST acquisition of Pegasus, confirms that civil society members were the primary target of Morocco from the very beginning of their Pegasus use in 2017,” Donncha Ó Cearbhaill, leader of the Security Lab told OCCRP.

According to the findings, the government's deployment of Pegasus evolved in tandem with the technological development in the spyware. Amnesty documented the use of sophisticated attack vectors, ranging from “one-click” phishing links requiring user interaction to advanced “zero-click” exploits capable of compromising devices without any action from the target.

title: U.K. Sanctions Four Georgians Over Occupied Ukraine Visit
content:
The U.K. has sanctioned four Georgians—including the brother-in-law of Tbilisi’s mayor—for “legitimising Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory” after they met with the head of a Russian-backed separatist republic.

The designations are part of a broader British sanctions package announced in response to intensifying Russian drone strikes against Ukraine in September. According to a press release Thursday, the wider measures target Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Kremlin propagandists, and individuals allegedly involved in human rights abuses against Ukrainian civilians. 

“The U.K. will not flinch in our support for Ukraine,” said Europe Minister Lord Wood of Anfield.

The U.K. sanctions notice states the four men “joined a delegation of Georgian politicians who met with the head of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, and subsequently publicised the visit.” All four now face U.K. asset freezes and travel bans.

The sanctioned delegates include political commentator Paata Abuladze, Mamuka Pipia, leader of the minor Solidarity for Peace party, party member Giorgi Iremadze, and Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, founder of a Georgian Russian-language TV channel.

title: Ex-Hungarian Minister Detained in $53 Million Graft Probe
content:
Black-masked law enforcement officers escorted Balázs Hankó, a former Hungarian culture minister, into a district court on Thursday, where a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention over allegations that he masterminded the widespread misappropriation of state funds to benefit the party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Hankó was taken into custody after Hungary's Parliament voted 139 to 0 on Monday to strip his legislative immunity. Before surrendering to prosecutors later that evening, he spent the day inside the Parliament building surrounded by his family, framing his pending arrest as political persecution.

"My conscience is clear; this is a political show trial," Hankó said in a video broadcast live on Orbán’s Facebook page before walking out alongside relatives and lawmakers from Fidesz, Orbán's right-wing party, which is now in opposition.

title: Raids Across Europe Target Far-Right Network Accused of Producing Neo-Nazi Music
content:
Authorities in five European countries carried out coordinated searches on Wednesday as part of an investigation into a suspected far-right criminal organization accused of producing and selling sound recordings containing music that incited hatred and spread National Socialist, antisemitic, racist and dehumanizing ideology.

The Rostock Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania State Office of Criminal Investigation said four suspects, aged 55, 52, 48 and 43, are being investigated for alleged membership in a criminal organization. One of them is also suspected of acting as its ringleader. The searches were carried out under warrants issued by an investigating judge at the Rostock Local Court.

Investigators suspect the four formed a permanent association no later than 2020 and worked together in an organized division of labor to produce and sell recordings containing hate-inciting music.

title: Leaked Warrant List Reveals How Turkmenistan Targets Critics Abroad
content:
Even as he bounced between Poland, Sweden and the Netherlands seeking political asylum, Nurmuhammet Annayev kept pressure on the authoritarian regime in his home country of Turkmenistan.

Annayev runs a YouTube channel that has brought him popularity among fellow critics of the Turkmenistan government. But his activism has also kept him firmly in the regime’s sights.

“Turns out they can even take people from abroad,” he said. “These guys are ready to eliminate — to disappear — the person standing in front of them to achieve their goals.”

Annayev, whose exact location OCCRP is not disclosing due to security reasons, is right to believe he is a target of Turkmenistan’s sprawling security and legal apparatus. 

OCCRP’s member center, Turkmen.news, has obtained an arrest warrant list from the Ministry of Internal Affairs showing that Annayev was wanted in his home country for political reasons. He was accused of “calls for an armed seizure of power or change of the constitutional order,” as well as “open calls for extremist activities.”

title: The US Blacklists Alleged Venezuelan Cyber Crime Mastermind
content:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Wednesday announced it had placed on a special blacklist Aníbal Alexander Canelón Aguirre— a Venezuelan who appears on the FBI’s "Ten Most Wanted" list—identifying him as a key link in a financial network for the notorious crime group Tren de Aragua. 

Canelón Aguirre is wanted by the Justice Department for allegedly leading a multi-million dollar ATM fraud scheme. Authorities accuse him of masterminding a jackpotting operation involving malware that when installed allows thieves to direct the bank machine to spew out money.

The alleged Venezuelan hacker topped a list of six Venezuelans and three Mexicans whose names were announced Wednesday as having been added to a group of specially designated nationals. It effectively locks them out of the global financial system. Six of the named are co-defendants of Canelón Aguirre in a U.S. prosecution.

The accused hacker has been on the run, lending his tech skills to the likes of a Romanian mafia operating along Mexico's white-sand beaches and became the cyber "engineer" of the infamous Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang.

title: Fiji Overhauls Evidence Security After 52 Kilos of Cocaine Vanish from Court
content:
Fiji’s police chief has ordered the immediate transfer of all illicit drugs and cash to highly secure police vaults after officials confirmed Wednesday that 52.4 kilograms of cocaine tied to two major criminal cases were stolen from a High Court evidence room, in the capital, Suva, with much of the contraband replaced by flour.

The incident is seen as a significant blow to a police force already struggling with corruption allegations amid a surge in international drug trafficking. However, Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu maintained that police are not responsible for guarding evidence once it is transferred to the judiciary, comparing the nation’s High Court to a private residence.

“It’s just like your home,” he told an OCCRP reporter. “You’re the boss of your home. I cannot come and tell you I’ll guard your home. Simple.”

Fiji, a nation of fewer than a million people, is facing an escalating drug crisis. It has become a transit hub for cocaine smuggled from South America to Australia and New Zealand, and is now seeing a spike in domestic use driving soaring HIV rates linked to intravenous methamphetamine use.
